chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, who raised it (as marfu') from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The judges are four: three are in the Fire and one is in Paradise — a man who judges with injustice and he knows, so he is in the Fire; a man who judges with injustice and he does not know, so he is in the Fire; a man who judges with the truth and he does not know, so he is in the Fire; and a man who judges with the truth and he does know, so he is in Paradise.
And he (peace be upon him) said: 'Judgment is of two kinds — the judgment of God and the judgment of Jahiliyya. So whoever errs in the judgment of God has judged by the judgment of Jahiliyya'.

key_terms.الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ: al-Jahiliyya — the pre-Islamic Age of Ignorance; here used as a category for any judgment not derived from divine law
key_terms.الْقُضَاةُ: al-qudah — judges, specifically those who hold judicial authority in Islamic law
key_terms.جَوْر: jawr — injustice, inequity, oppression; the opposite of 'adl (justice)
key_terms.رَفَعَهُ: rafa'ahu — he raised it; technical hadith term indicating a mursal/marfu' chain where an intermediate narrator is omitted

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Sadiq say about the four types of judges and their fate in the afterlife?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) categorizes judges into four types, three destined for Hellfire and only one for Paradise. The key criterion is not merely reaching the correct outcome, but possessing the requisite knowledge ('ilm) to judge rightly — ignorant judgment, even when accidentally correct, is condemned. The second statement reinforces that all judgment falls into one of two categories: divine law or pre-Islamic tribal custom (Jahiliyya), with any deviation from divine law constituting the latter.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Khalid, from his father,

(It has been) narrated from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>: ‘The judges are four, three are in the Fire, and one in the Paradise – a man who judges with inequity and he knows, so he is in the Fire; and a man judges with inequity and he does not know, so he is in the Fire; and a man who judges with the truth and he does not know, so he is in the Fire; and a man who judges with the truth and he does know, so he is in the Paradise’.

And he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The judgements are two judgements – a judgement of Allah<sup>azwj</sup>, and a judgement of the ignorance. So the one who errs in the Judgements of Allah<sup>azwj</sup>, has judged by the judgement of the ignorance (disbelief)’.
en.sarwar: 1. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from his father in a marfu ‘ manner who has narrated the following: “Abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘Judges are of four kinds of whom three are in the fire and one is in the garden (paradises). There is a man who issues judgments unjustly and he knows it, so he is in the fire. There is a man who issues judgments unjustly but he does not know, he also is in the fire; and there is a man who issues judgments that are right but he does not have the knowledge, he also is in the fire. There is a man who issues the right kind of judgments, based on his right knowledge, thus he is in the garden (paradises).’

“He (the Imam), ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘Judgments are of two kinds: the judgments under rules of Allah and the judgments of ignorance. If one misses the law and judgment of Allah, he then has judged by the judgment of ignorance.’”
